blocks.text: Stop 1: Day and night, and the seasons

blocks.markdown:
The **Sun** is a star. Earth **orbits** it once a year.

Earth **rotates** once in 24 hours, which gives us day and night.
blocks.say: The Sun is a star. It is the centre of our solar system, and Earth is one of the planets that travel around it. Earth spins like a top. It takes twenty-four hours to spin once, and this spin is what gives us day and night. The side of Earth facing the Sun has daytime. The side facing away has night. Earth also travels around the Sun once every year, and its tilt gives us the seasons.

scenes.caption: Facing the Sun: day.
scenes.say: Earth spins. The side facing the Sun has day, and Pakistan sees the Sun rise in the morning.

scenes.caption: Facing away: night.
scenes.say: As Earth keeps turning, our side faces away from the Sun, and it becomes night.

question.explanation: Earth rotates, so different places face the Sun at different times.

blocks.markdown:
The Moon is a **satellite** that orbits Earth.

The Moon reflects sunlight. Its **phases** change over about a month.
blocks.say: The Moon is a natural satellite, which means it orbits a planet. It orbits Earth about once a month. The Moon does not make its own light. We see it because it reflects light from the Sun. As the Moon travels around Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half. These are called the phases of the Moon, such as the new moon, the crescent, the half moon and the full moon. Muslims use the sighting of the new crescent moon to mark the start of each month in the Islamic calendar.

scenes.caption: Crescent moon.
scenes.say: A thin crescent moon. Only a small part of the lit half faces us.

scenes.caption: Full moon.
scenes.say: A full moon. The whole lit half faces us, so it looks like a bright circle.

sub_lessons.title: Forces: gravity, friction and air resistance

blocks.markdown:
A **force** is a push or a pull.

**Gravity** pulls objects towards the centre of Earth.
blocks.say: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down or change direction. Gravity is a force that pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth. It is why things fall down when you drop them, and why we stay on the ground. We measure forces in newtons, using a forcemeter. A heavier object has more weight, because gravity pulls it harder.

scenes.caption: Gravity pulls things down.
scenes.say: An apple falls from a tree. Gravity pulls it down towards the ground.

scenes.caption: Heavier means a bigger pull.
scenes.say: A heavier object is pulled harder. We measure the pull in newtons.

question.prompt: Which force pulls things towards the Earth?
question.explanation: Gravity pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth.

blocks.title: Rough or smooth?
blocks.goal: Put surfaces with lots of friction in High and surfaces with little friction in Low.
blocks.say: Friction is a force between two surfaces that rub together. It slows things down. A rough surface such as carpet has lots of friction, and a smooth surface such as ice has very little. Air resistance and water resistance are forces that push against things moving through air or water. A parachute has a large surface, so it catches lots of air and falls slowly. A fair test of parachutes changes only the size of the canopy, and keeps the weight and drop height the same.

blocks.markdown:
Earth has layers: the **crust**, the **mantle** and the **core**.

The crust is broken into slow moving **tectonic plates**.
blocks.say: Earth is made of layers, like a peach. On the outside is the crust, a thin layer of rock where we live. Under the crust is the mantle, which is a thick layer of hot rock. At the centre is the core, which is extremely hot and made mostly of iron. The crust is broken into huge pieces called tectonic plates. These plates move very slowly, only a few centimetres a year. Look at the layers.

scenes.caption: The crust.
scenes.say: The crust is the thin outer layer, where we live.

scenes.caption: The mantle and core.
scenes.say: Under the crust is a thick layer of hot rock called the mantle. In the centre is the very hot core.

question.prompt: Which is the thin, outer layer of the Earth?
question.explanation: The crust is the thin outer layer of rock.

blocks.title: Earth words
blocks.say: Where plates push against each other, rub past each other or pull apart, we find volcanoes and earthquakes. A volcano erupts when hot melted rock, called magma, rises up and bursts out. Once it is above ground, we call it lava. An earthquake is a shaking of the ground when plates suddenly move. Pakistan sits near the edge of two plates, so it can have earthquakes. Scientists measure them to help keep people safe. Try a memory game, then see if you can match the words.

sub_lessons.title: Forces and safety in real life

blocks.text: Stop 1: Using forces to stay safe

blocks.markdown:
Forces help us stay safe: **seat belts**, **brakes** and **helmets**.

Friction helps brakes and tyres to grip.
blocks.say: We use what we know about forces every day. Seat belts hold us in our seats when a car stops suddenly. Brakes use friction to slow down a bike or a car, and tyres with a good grip give more friction on the road. Bike helmets protect our heads if we fall. Crumple zones in cars soak up a crash. A skydiver uses a parachute to increase air resistance. All of them help to keep people safe.

blocks.alt: Seat belts, brakes and helmets keep us safe.
blocks.caption: Seat belts, brakes and helmets keep us safe.
blocks.say: Seat belts, brakes and helmets all use what we know about forces.

question.prompt: What do brakes use to slow a bike down?
question.explanation: Brakes rub against the wheel, and friction slows it.

blocks.title: My family safety plan
instructions: Draw a plan of your home. Mark strong tables and the exits.
Choose a meeting place outside, away from buildings.
Practise Drop, Cover and Hold with your family.
blocks.say: Earthquakes can be frightening, but knowing what to do keeps us safe. If the ground shakes, drop to the ground, take cover under a strong table, and hold on. Stay away from windows and heavy furniture. When the shaking stops, walk outside carefully to an open space, away from buildings. We remember the people who were hurt in earthquakes, and we pray for them and help in any way we can. Make a family plan.
